title: What is the PACELC theorem and how does it extend CAP — during a network Partition choose Availability or Consistency (same as CAP), but Else (when the system is running normally with no partition) you still face a trade-off between Latency and Consistency — and why does this matter (CAP only talks about failure mode, but most of the time the system is healthy and the real daily trade-off is "do I wait for all replicas to ack (consistent but slower) or return after one ack (fast but possibly stale)") — e.g. DynamoDB is PA/EL (available during partition, low-latency normally), PostgreSQL synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent always, at the cost of latency)?
shortTitle: PACELC Theorem — Extending CAP to the Healthy-System Case

s1_definition.profdef: PACELC extends CAP by adding the normal-operation case. It states: if there is a Partition (P), the system must choose between Availability and Consistency (A or C) — this is exactly CAP; Else (E), when the system is running normally with no partition, it must still choose between Latency and Consistency (L or C). So a system is classified by two letters, like PA/EL or PC/EC, describing its behavior both during a partition and during healthy operation.
s1_definition.analogy: CAP only describes what the National Bank of India does when the phone line between branches breaks. But the line is fine almost all the time, and even then there is a choice: when Rajesh updates his balance, do the branches wait until every branch confirms the new number before telling him "done" (consistent but slower), or does the nearest branch say "done" immediately and tell the others later (fast but the others are briefly out of date)? PACELC adds that everyday trade-off — latency versus consistency when all is well — to the partition trade-off CAP already covered.
s1_definition.oneliner: PACELC = during a Partition choose A or C (like CAP), Else during normal operation choose Latency or Consistency — it covers the healthy case CAP ignores.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** PACELC extends CAP by adding the normal-operation case. It states: if there is a Partition (P), the system must choose between Availability and Consistency (A or C) — this is exactly CAP; Else (E), when the system is running normally with no partition, it must still choose between Latency and Consistency (L or C). So a system is classified by two letters, like PA/EL or PC/EC, describing its behavior both during a partition and during healthy operation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** CAP only describes what the National Bank of India does when the phone line between branches breaks. But the line is fine almost all the time, and even then there is a choice: when Rajesh updates his balance, do the branches wait until every branch confirms the new number before telling him "done" (consistent but slower), or does the nearest branch say "done" immediately and tell the others later (fast but the others are briefly out of date)? PACELC adds that everyday trade-off — latency versus consistency when all is well — to the partition trade-off CAP already covered.

**One line to remember:** PACELC = during a Partition choose A or C (like CAP), Else during normal operation choose Latency or Consistency — it covers the healthy case CAP ignores.

sections.s2_technical:
CAP has a blind spot: it only describes behavior during a network partition, which is the rare failure mode. But a well-run system is partitioned a tiny fraction of the time; the overwhelming majority of its life it is healthy. CAP says nothing about the trade-offs you face then. PACELC, proposed by Daniel Abadi, fills that gap by stating the trade-off in both regimes.

The "PA/PC" half is the partition case, identical to CAP: when the network splits, you either stay Available (serve on both sides, risk divergence) or stay Consistent (refuse or block to avoid divergence). The "EL/EC" half is the new part: Else — in the normal, no-partition state — you still choose between Latency and Consistency. Why is there a trade-off even with a healthy network? Because data is replicated across multiple nodes, and when a write arrives you must decide how many replicas must acknowledge it before you tell the client "done." If you wait for all (or a quorum of) replicas to acknowledge, every subsequent read is guaranteed to see the write — strong consistency — but the client waits longer for every slow replica, so latency is higher. If you acknowledge after just one replica (the local one) and propagate to the others in the background, the client gets a fast response, but a read hitting a not-yet-updated replica could see stale data — lower latency, weaker consistency.

So a system is labeled with two choices. PostgreSQL with synchronous replication is PC/EC: during a partition it favors consistency (the primary refuses writes it cannot replicate), and in normal operation it also favors consistency by waiting for the replica to acknowledge before committing, accepting higher latency. DynamoDB in its default tunable configuration is PA/EL: during a partition it stays available, and in normal operation it favors low latency by acknowledging quickly and replicating asynchronously, accepting that reads may be eventually consistent (though it also offers an optional strongly-consistent read). Cassandra is likewise typically PA/EL but is tunable per request via consistency levels (ONE for low latency, QUORUM or ALL for stronger consistency). MongoDB with majority write concern leans PC/EC; with weaker write concern it leans toward EL.

Why this matters practically: the daily, always-present engineering decision is the EL-versus-EC one, because partitions are rare but every single write faces the "wait for all acks or return after one" question. CAP-only thinking leads teams to reason solely about the rare failure case and ignore the latency-versus-staleness trade-off that actually dominates their p99 latency and their read-your-writes behavior every day. The senior insight is that PACELC makes you specify behavior in both regimes and, like CAP, it should be applied per operation: a balance update can be EC (synchronous, consistent) while a feed read can be EL (fast, eventually consistent). Many databases expose this as tunable consistency levels or write concerns, so you set it per query rather than globally.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India replicates data across three nodes. For balance writes the team wants PC/EC behavior: wait for a quorum to acknowledge so any later read is correct, even though it is slower. For the activity feed they want EL behavior: acknowledge after one node for speed, tolerating brief staleness. Previously everything used fast single-ack writes (EL) to chase low latency, and a balance read right after a write sometimes hit a lagging replica and showed the old balance, confusing customers — a classic EL-versus-EC mistake applied to the wrong data.

Our mini-project models a replicated write with a configurable acknowledgment policy: `QUORUM` (consistent, higher latency) versus `ONE` (fast, possibly stale). A `Demo` writes a balance with QUORUM and a feed event with ONE, showing the latency and staleness difference.

The code will contain: a `Replica` with a lagging apply, a `ReplicatedStore` with a write method taking a consistency level, and a `Demo` comparing QUORUM and ONE writes with a subsequent read.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three replicas r1, r2, r3. One balance write with QUORUM (EC) and one feed write with ONE (EL).

Step 1: The balance write uses QUORUM. The store applies the value synchronously to a majority of replicas (r1 and r2) before acknowledging. This costs more time because it waits for the majority, which is the EC choice — higher latency for guaranteed correctness.

Step 2: Immediately after the QUORUM write acknowledges, a read from r2 already shows the new balance, because r2 was in the synchronous quorum. This is read-your-writes consistency, the benefit of EC, which is exactly what a balance needs.

Step 3: The feed write uses ONE. The store applies the value to r1 only and acknowledges immediately, propagating to r2 and r3 in the background. This returns faster — the EL choice, low latency.

Step 4: Immediately after the ONE write, a read from r3 may still show the old value because r3 has not caught up yet — brief staleness, the cost of EL. This is acceptable for a feed.

Step 5: After a short wait, r3 catches up and shows the new feed value. The demo prints the latency difference and the staleness window, showing EC for balances and EL for feeds.

```
Oct 25, 2026 17:02:00 INFO: EC write (QUORUM) acked after majority applied
EC (balance) latency=2ms, read r2=balance=50000
Oct 25, 2026 17:02:00 INFO: EL write (ONE) acked after single replica
EL (feed) latency=0ms, read r3 (maybe stale)=balance=50000
EL (feed) read r3 after lag catches up=feed=login
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  WRITE during HEALTHY network (the "Else" case PACELC adds)
    │
    ├─ EC (QUORUM): apply to majority SYNC, then ack
    │     r1 r2 (ack) ... r3 async
    │     read r2 right away → NEW value (consistent)  ← higher latency
    │
    └─ EL (ONE): apply to r1, ack immediately, others async
          r1 (ack) ... r2,r3 async (lagging)
          read r3 right away → OLD value (stale) → later catches up  ← low latency
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  During PARTITION (the CAP case): PA (stay available) vs PC (stay consistent)
```

The architecture assigns PC/EC storage to money and PA/EL storage to cosmetic data, and where the engine allows, tunes consistency per request.

sections.s6_takeaway:
PACELC extends CAP by covering the normal-operation case that CAP ignores. It says: if there is a Partition, you choose between Availability and Consistency, which is exactly CAP; Else, when the network is healthy, you still choose between Latency and Consistency. So a system is labeled with two letters, like PA/EL or PC/EC. The reason the Else half matters is that partitions are rare — a well-run system is healthy almost all the time — yet even then there is an unavoidable trade-off, because data is replicated and every write must decide how many replicas acknowledge before returning. If you wait for a quorum or all replicas, every later read is guaranteed correct but latency is higher; if you acknowledge after one replica and propagate the rest asynchronously, you return fast but a read on a lagging replica can be stale. CAP-only thinking fixates on the rare failure mode and ignores this everyday latency-versus-staleness decision that actually dominates p99 latency and read-your-writes behavior.

Concretely, PostgreSQL with synchronous replication is PC/EC — consistent during a partition and consistent in normal operation by waiting for replica acknowledgment, at the cost of latency — while DynamoDB in its default mode is PA/EL — available during a partition and low-latency normally with eventually-consistent reads, though it offers an optional strongly-consistent read. Cassandra is tunable per request through consistency levels like ONE versus QUORUM. In our National Bank of India system we classify per operation: balance writes are EC, so we wait for a quorum and a read right after a write is correct, while feed and counter writes are EL, acknowledged after one replica for speed with brief staleness that is harmless. Previously everything used fast single-ack writes to chase low latency, and a balance read right after a write sometimes hit a lagging replica and showed the old balance, which we fixed by making balances EC. The line I remember is: during a partition choose A or C like CAP, else choose latency or consistency, and apply it per operation — EC for money, EL for feeds.
